newsitem.title: USA: US policy seen on hold in July--Ex Boston Fed head.
newsitem.headline: US policy seen on hold in July--Ex Boston Fed head.

text.p: The Federal Reserve is likely to keep monetary policy unchanged at its policy-setting meeting July 1-2 in response to a slowing economy in the second quarter, a former Fed official said.
"I don't think they're going to do anything," Richard Syron, former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Syron believes the economy slowed substantially in the second quarter after a sizzling 5.9 percent growth rate in the first three months of 1997. But the former Boston Fed head said he expects the economy to rebound in the third quarter.
"I think the economy could easily get some strengthening coming back in the third quarter and beyond," Syron said.

Syron, who now chairs the American Stock Exchange, said he expects gross domestic product growth to jump back to around 4.0 percent in the third quarter. Most analysts expect second quarter growth of around 2.0 percent.
Syron said a 4.0-percent growth rate is was not sustainable for a long period of time and would likely prompt the Fed to hike interest rates later in the year.
The ex-Boston Fed chief said continuation of tight labor markets would be one of the leading forces driving the economic rebound in the third quarter.

"I tend to look at the labor market, and the labor market still is pretty tight. We haven't seen any real wage pressures, but at some point you can't help it; one way or the other, there will be a little bit (of pressure)," he said.
Syron cited a jump in the Chicagoland Business Barometer (CBB) in June as another indication that the economy might be poised to bounce back in the second half of the year.
"All of this is consistent with the notion that the economy slowing in the second quarter doesn't necessarily mean it's going to keep slowing," he said.
The CBB, released on Monday by the Purchasing Management Association of Chicago, surged to 61.5 in June from 56.8 in May. A reading above 50 suggests expansion.
A drop in the prices-paid component of the report, however, showed inflation still appears subdued at the manufacturing level. The prices index fell to 53.7 from 56.9 in May.
